boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Campbell's Station record (November 16, 1863) in Longstreet's Knoxville Campaign [November-December 1863]. The Huff's Ferry and Lenoir's actions of November 14–15 are outside the frozen interval. The siege, the November 23–25 actions, the pursuit and campaign-wide figures are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field names the Department of the Ohio and the Confederate forces in East Tennessee without counts; the live field reads zero. Burnside wrote in 1865 that his command was little over 5,000 against an enemy at least double, and on November 17 that Longstreet had crossed with about 15,000. Longstreet says he planned the move with 20,000 and accepts Stevenson's figure of 23,000 for Burnside's force on entering East Tennessee. NPS says Longstreet had two divisions and about 5,000 cavalry.
claims.rationale: Each commander gives the opponent the larger number; the figures differ in date and scope. None is adopted. Live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: NPS says Campbell's Station lay where the Concord road met the Kingston road to Knoxville. Burnside says White's division stood on rising ground south of the road, that high ground on his left commanded the position, and that he withdrew to a ridge about three-quarters of a mile to the rear. Longstreet says the enemy took a strong position east of the station and then a more commanding one about a mile back.
claims.rationale: Positions chosen on the day and ground from interested accounts; no map verification.

claims.value: NPS says Burnside hoped to reach the crossroads first and continue to Knoxville, while Longstreet meant to hold it and force a fight outside the works. Burnside says Hartranft's division was sent to seize the forks of the road. Longstreet says McLaws was ordered to intercept the retreating enemy at Campbell's Station, and that his plan was to crush Burnside's force before it knew his purpose.
claims.rationale: Stated aims from a summary and interested accounts; not a causal estimate.

claims.value: Longstreet says that had Jenkins attacked the flank in time the Union force must have been destroyed, and that Jenkins attributes his failure to mismanagement by Law. NPS says Jenkins's division maneuvered ineffectively. Burnside says he gave the order to withdraw at 2 p.m. The frozen commanders are Lieutenant General Longstreet and Major General Burnside; the live heading ranks Longstreet Major General.
claims.rationale: Judgments and a counterfactual are attributed; the frozen commanders do not receive automatic sole credit, and the live rank is not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Union victory. NPS says the Confederates suspended the attack while Burnside continued to Knoxville. Burnside says the new position was taken without the slightest confusion and his command withdrew to Knoxville after nightfall; Longstreet says the enemy drew off after dark.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live casualty fields give 970 (US 400; CS 570). Burnside's 1865 report puts his killed, wounded and missing at about 300 and says the enemy's loss must have been very severe.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

open_questions: White's, Potter's, McLaws's and Jenkins's reports and the returns remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Burnside's, Parke's and Longstreet's reports, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XXXI, Part 1, are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; the volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Burnside's full report was written in November 1865 and Longstreet's in January 1864. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
